body_text: Strattec President and CEO to Participate in CES Panel on AI and OEM-Supplier Collaboration January 5, 2026 PDF Version MILWAUKEE--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jan. 5, 2026-- Strattec Security Corporation (Nasdaq: STRT) (“Company”), a leading provider of smart vehicle access, security and authorization solutions for the global automotive industry, announced today that Jennifer Slater, President & CEO, will be a participant on a panel at CES on Tuesday, January 6 at 11:00 am PT . The panel, which is sponsored by the Boston Consulting Group, is titled “Smarter Together: AI, Cost & the Future of OEM-Supplier Collaboration”. The panel will discuss how the traditional OEM–supplier relationship is evolving and how both parties can better leverage AI and new forms of collaboration to drive win-win outcomes to better position the industry to thrive in an increasingly uncertain world. Ms. Slater’s participation underscores Strattec’s commitment to the advancement of digital transformation in the automotive industry and reflects the Company’s strong collaboration and long-standing relationships with OEM partners. In addition to Ms. Slater, speakers on the panel will include Brian Colliee, Managing Director and Senior Partner, Boston Consulting Group, Paul Farrell, EVP-CSO, BorgWarner and Peter Holdmann, Member of the Board of Management, ZF Group. About CES (Consumer Electronic Show) CES® is the world’s leading technology showcase, where global innovators, business leaders, and investors convene to explore emerging technologies shaping the future of industry and society. The event is produced by the Consumer Technology Association (CTA)®. About Strattec Strattec is a leading global provider of advanced automotive access, security & authorization solutions for leading vehicle manufacturers, primarily in the U.S. For over 110 years, Strattec has pioneered innovations in vehicle security, transitioning from mechanical to integrated electro-mechanical systems. Its highly engineered products include power access solutions, latches, vehicle start systems, keys, fobs & accessories, locks & locksets, door handles and other access products. Power access solutions provide the motion control for power liftgates, sliding power doors and power tailgates. For more information on Strattec and its solutions, visit www.strattec.com . title: What is the difference between convergent and divergent thinking?
summary: Discover how divergent and convergent thinking shapes problem-solving in ADHD. Learn strategies to harness creative potential while enhancing focus for better productivity and success.
body_text: Ever had a brilliant idea pop into your head during a brainstorming session, only to hit a mental brick wall when trying to figure out how to turn that idea into reality? If so, you’ve likely experienced the tension between divergent and convergent thinking — two cognitive styles that work together like yin and yang but sometimes feel worlds apart, especially for people with adult ADHD. For many, ADHD is a superpower that fuels creativity and out-of-the-box solutions, but it can also lead to frustration when focus is needed to make those ideas actionable. Understanding the balance between divergent thinking and convergent thinking is key to unlocking your full potential. Here's a look at both thinking styles, how they show up in ADHD brains, and why knowing when to switch gears can make all the difference in navigating the challenges of adult ADHD. ⬇️ What is convergent thinking? Convergent thinking is the process of narrowing down ideas and finding the most practical solution. It’s focused, structured, and logical. Imagine planning a road trip: you begin with many possible routes, but with convergent thinking, you decide on the best one based on traffic, distance, and stops along the way. This type of thinking helps you make decisions and complete tasks efficiently. In day-to-day life, convergent thinking is essential for: Making and following a budget Deciding where to eat based on reviews and preferences Solving a math problem or a puzzle However, for people with adult ADHD, convergent thinking can be difficult. ADHD can make it hard to maintain focus, follow through, and organize thoughts. This can lead to frustration when you need to make concrete decisions or execute ideas. ↘️ What is divergent thinking? Divergent thinking is all about generating ideas and exploring multiple possibilities. It’s the kind of thinking that happens during a brainstorming session, where you start with a blank slate and come up with as many solutions or ideas as possible. Unlike convergent thinking, which narrows options down, divergent thinking encourages expansion and creativity. Divergent thinking thrives in situations like: Brainstorming ideas for a new project or business Creating art or writing a story Developing innovative solutions to challenges For individuals with ADHD, divergent thinking often comes naturally. The ADHD brain craves novelty and variety, making it easy to jump from one idea to the next. This kind of creativity can be a huge asset in fields like art, design, entrepreneurship, and writing. However, without the balance of convergent thinking, it can be hard to filter these ideas into actionable plans. 🧠 How do convergent and divergent thinking show up in ADHD? For those with ADHD, the balance between these two thinking styles can be tricky. Many people with ADHD excel at divergent thinking due to their natural curiosity and creative minds. But when it’s time to focus, narrow down choices, and make decisions, the ADHD brain may struggle with the sustained focus and organization that convergent thinking demands. This creates a cycle of generating exciting ideas without the ability to fully execute them, leading to feelings of frustration or underachievement. 💪 How can you strengthen convergent thinking with ADHD? Fortunately, to improve focus and execution there are tools and techniques to strengthen convergent thinking: Break tasks into smaller steps: Instead of trying to complete a large project all at once, divide it into smaller, manageable parts. Use productivity tools: Checklists, planners, and timers designed for task management can help you stay on track. Practice time-blocking: Dedicate specific periods of time to convergent tasks like decision-making or project execution, and separate those from brainstorming sessions. Work in bursts: Short, focused work sessions followed by breaks can help maintain attention. The Pomodoro technique (25 minutes of work followed by a five-minute break) is especially effective. Get support: ADHD coaching can help create personalized plans to organize tasks and improve focus. An ADHD coach can offer guidance and strategies to balance creative thinking with practical execution. ⚖️ How can ADHD brains balance convergent and divergent thinking? The key to success with ADHD is knowing when to use each thinking style. Divergent thinking is perfect for situations where creativity is needed, like brainstorming a new project or tackling an open-ended problem. Convergent thinking, on the other hand, is necessary when you need to focus, make decisions, or complete tasks. Here’s how to strike the right balance: Start with divergent thinking : Use brainstorming sessions, mind mapping, or freewriting to generate as many ideas as possible. Let your creativity flow without judgment. Transition to convergent thinking: Once you’ve got a list of ideas, switch gears to narrowing them down. Use checklists, prioritize options, and focus on the most feasible and impactful ideas. Set clear goals: Whether using divergent or convergent thinking, setting clear goals can keep you on track. For divergent thinking sessions, aim to generate a certain number of ideas. For convergent thinking sessions, focus on making specific decisions or completing tasks. Use external tools: Tools like checklists, timelines, or prioritization matrices can help bring structure to your ideas and keep you accountable. Bottom line Finding the balance between convergent and divergent thinking can be transformative, especially for individuals with ADHD. Understanding when to tap into creative exploration and when to apply structured focus can help unlock new levels of productivity and success. Take a moment to reflect on your own thinking habits. Are you leveraging both modes effectively? Start by incorporating divergent tools like brainstorming and mind mapping into your idea generation. Then, use checklists, timelines, or other convergent tools to filter those ideas and bring them to life. Begin experimenting today, and see how embracing this balance can help you achieve more — both personally and professionally! ‍

title: Beginner's guide to SMART goals for ADHD
summary: Learn how SMART goals can help adults with ADHD turn overwhelming ambitions into actionable, achievable plans with clarity, structure, and flexibility.
body_text: For adults with ADHD, setting goals is often the easy part. With a knack for creativity and out-of-the box thinking, they often have ideas aplenty. And in the beginning, especially, the excitement borne of novelty makes the sudden decision to learn to play the accordion or finally get into an exercise routine feel easy enough. The next day, though, when it’s time to follow through…that’s when things get sticky. The problem isn’t a lack of effort or desire, though; it’s the absence of a system designed to bridge the gaps created by ADHD’s challenges, such as staying focused, following through, and organizing priorities. That’s where the SMART goal framework comes in. Unlike vague aspirations that quickly lose steam, SMART goals focus on clarity and structure. By ensuring that your goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound, this method transforms overwhelming ambitions into actionable plans. It’s a process that helps you focus your energy on what matters most, making progress feel even more possible. In this post, we’ll show you how to use the SMART framework to turn scattered thoughts into focused actions. With this approach, goal-setting becomes less about struggling to stay afloat and more about confidently moving forward. What are SMART goals? SMART goals are a powerful tool to transform your ambitions into achievable outcomes. The acronym stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Each element plays a vital role in creating a structured, ADHD-friendly plan that turns overwhelming dreams into clear, actionable steps. Here’s a detailed breakdown of each component: 🎯Specific A common pitfall for people with adult ADHD is setting goals that are too broad or undefined, which makes it hard to know where to start. “I want to be healthier” is an example of a vague wish — it’s well-intentioned but lacks clarity. Pro tip: Break goals down into a concrete, actionable target. For instance, “I will exercise for 30 minutes three times a week” gives you a clear plan to follow. This specificity reduces decision fatigue and helps you focus on a single, manageable action. 📏 Measurable Without a way to track your progress, it’s easy to lose momentum or feel like you’re getting nowhere. ADHD brains thrive on visible milestones and tangible results that provide a sense of achievement. Pro tip: Add clear metrics to your goal. Instead of saying, “I want to read more,” try “I’ll record how many pages I read each day, aiming to increase by at least five pages by the end of the week.” This allows you to track progress, celebrate wins, and stay motivated! 🏆 Achievable While aiming high can be exciting, overly ambitious goals often lead to burnout or discouragement, especially when adult ADHD is part of the equation. It’s important to set goals that stretch you just enough without overwhelming you. Pro tip: Consider your current resources and limitations. If you’re new to exercise, don’t commit to running a marathon next month. Instead, start with a goal like “I’ll walk for 15 minutes every morning.” This builds confidence and creates a foundation for future growth. 👌 Relevant Goals are most effective when they resonate with your personal priorities and what genuinely matters to you. For someone with ADHD, pursuing goals that don’t feel meaningful can lead to boredom and procrastination. Pro tip: Reflect on why the goal matters. For example, if you want to save money, think about how it ties to your values: “I’ll save $50 each week to afford a weekend trip that helps me recharge.” When goals align with your core motivations, staying committed becomes much easier! ⏳ Time-bound For ADHD brains, deadlines can be both a blessing and a curse. Without a timeline, it’s easy to procrastinate. However, too much pressure can trigger anxiety or avoidance. The key is to create a balanced sense of urgency. Pro tip: Add a realistic deadline to your goal. Instead of saying, “I’ll clean the house,” try “I’ll clean the living room by 5 p.m. today.” Breaking larger deadlines into smaller, manageable checkpoints can also help you stay on track without feeling overwhelmed. Why do SMART goals work for ADHD? Managing goals can be uniquely challenging for adults with ADHD due to difficulties with executive function, time management , and task initiation. SMART goals provide a framework that directly addresses these hurdles. Here’s why they work so well: 🏗️ Structure simplifies complex planning: SMART goals turn big, overwhelming ideas into clear, actionable steps, making it easier to plan, prioritize, and organize without the stress caused by executive dysfunction. 🥅 Clear goals eliminate overthinking: Measurable outcomes reduce ambiguity, providing a straightforward path to success. With defined metrics, you can focus on progress rather than being bogged down by indecision. ⏱️ Deadlines counteract time blindness: Time-bound goals introduce realistic timelines that help you stay on track, prevent procrastination, and maintain focus without adding unnecessary pressure. 🪜 Concrete steps ease task initiation: Specific goals offer clear starting points, making it simpler to transition from intention to action — an essential aid for overcoming ADHD-related difficulties with starting tasks. 🤏 Smaller milestones make big goals achievable: Breaking down larger objectives into manageable steps reduces overwhelm and fosters a sense of accomplishment, helping you maintain momentum toward your ultimate goal. How do SMART goals work for ADHD adults? While SMART goals provide structure, tailoring them to ADHD-specific needs can enhance their effectiveness. Here are strategies to optimize SMART goals for greater success: Embrace flexibility within your plan. Allow for adjustments and revisions as you work through your goals, keeping the process adaptable to your needs while maintaining focus on the end result. Plan for extra time to handle the unexpected. Incorporate buffer periods into deadlines to account for delays or shifts in attention, reducing pressure and improving your chances of completion. Motivate yourself with built-in rewards. Celebrate progress by rewarding yourself for achieving milestones, reinforcing positive habits and maintaining enthusiasm. Leverage support through accountability partners. Work with a trusted friend, ADHD coach , or group to stay focused and motivated. Regular check-ins or body doubling sessions can help sustain your efforts. Use visual tools to track progress. You can use charts, calendars, or lists to create a clear visual representation of your progress, helping you stay organized and motivated. Incorporate sensory cues to engage your brain. Enhance your goal-tracking system with sensory elements like colorful markers, stickers, or tactile tools to make the process more engaging and enjoyable. Why are SMART goals hard for adults with ADHD? While SMART goals offer a clear framework for achieving objectives, they may not be the best framework for all individuals with ADHD. Here are a few potential drawbacks for this framework, and how they might manifest: The rigid structure can feel restrictive. A SMART goal thrives on specificity and structure, but for ADHD brains that crave flexibility and novelty, this rigidity can feel stifling. The linear, step-by-step approach can make the process feel more like a chore than a motivator, dampening enthusiasm and creativity. Overthinking the setup instead of taking action. ADHD’s tendency to hyperfocus can backfire when crafting SMART goals. Instead of moving forward, you might get stuck tweaking the “perfect” wording or debating whether your goal is specific or measurable enough. This perfectionism in planning can delay the actual steps needed to achieve your goals. Time constraints can clash with time blindness. One of the most common ADHD challenges is time blindness — losing track of how long things take or struggling to estimate durations accurately. SMART goals rely on time-bound deadlines which can feel overwhelming or unrealistic, leading to missed targets or unnecessary stress. Inconsistent energy levels disrupt progress. ADHD energy levels can fluctuate wildly. One day, you’re brimming with motivation; the next, even small tasks feel insurmountable. SMART goals often assume a consistent pace and effort, which doesn’t align with these ups and downs, making the goals feel unattainable at times. Perfectionism and all-or-nothing thinking can take over. A SMART goal emphasizes precision and measurable outcomes, which can exacerbate perfectionism . For someone with ADHD, this might spiral into an all-or-nothing mindset. If the goal isn’t met exactly as planned, it’s seen as a failure. This rigidity can undermine the progress that’s actually been made. Your ADHD-friendly SMART goal template Creating your first SMART goal can be tricky when ADHD is in the mix, but don’t worry — we’ve got you covered! Here’s a simple, flexible template and tailored SMART goal examples to help you set goals ADHD style . 📝 Step 1: Use the formula Here’s a straightforward formula with examples of how to revise a general goal to SMART format: Specific : What exactly do you want to accomplish? General goal : I want to start reading more. SMART goal example : “I want to read for 15 minutes every day.” Measurable : How will you track your progress? General goal : I want to get stronger. SMART goal example : “Every Monday for the next 8 weeks, I’ll record my maximum number of push-ups and aim to improve that number by at least 2 reps each week.” Achievable : Is this realistic for where you are right now? General goal : I want to read a whole book every week. SMART goal example : “It’s manageable to read for 15 minutes, even on a busy day.” Relevant : Why is this goal important to you? General goal : I want to spend less time on my phone. SMART goal example : “I want to build a reading habit to help me relax and learn new things.” Time-bound : What’s your timeline? General goal : I want to build better habits. SMART goal example : “I’ll stick to this plan for the next 30 days and then re-evaluate.” 🚧 Step 2: Troubleshoot common obstacles Sometimes, even the best plans hit snags. Here’s how to troubleshoot: Feeling overwhelmed? Break the goal into smaller, bite-sized steps. Instead of “read for 15 minutes,” start with “find a book I’m excited about.” Struggling with time blindness? P air the goal with an existing routine (e.g., “I’ll read after breakfast”). Low-energy days making it hard? Have a backup plan. On tougher days, swap reading for listening to an audiobook—it still counts! Hyperfocus derailing balance? Set a timer to count down from 15 minutes to zero, and place it far enough away that you need to stop reading and get up to turn it off. 💡Step 3: Make it your own Guess what? You don’t have to follow the SMART framework perfectly! Here’s how to adapt it to suit your ADHD brain: Tweak the rules : Adjust timelines, focus on progress over precision, or skip steps that don’t feel helpful. Make it fun : Use colorful sticky notes, doodles, or stickers to personalize your goal-tracking system. Be kind to yourself : It’s okay if your goals change. Treat each attempt as a learning experience, not a failure. From ADHD struggles to SMART success With ADHD, the key to success lies in embracing flexibility, celebrating small wins, and remembering that tools like SMART goals are here to help, not constrain you. Don’t feel pressured to follow every step of the framework to the letter. Instead, tweak it, play with it, and make it work for you. Whether that means focusing on just one or two elements at first, adding a bit of creativity, or prioritizing what feels most relevant, the important thing is to start. So, why wait? Pick one goal today — something simple, meaningful, and achievable. Adapt it using what you’ve learned, and take that first small step. Progress is progress, no matter how small. ‍

title: The slop is out of the bottle
summary: AI code “slop” is here to stay. The fix is human judgment: define contracts, test first, verify instantly, and stop shipping unreviewed output.
body_text: “Of course, this code is complete AI slop.” LaurieWired And so it will be, forever. The slop is out of the bottle. And just like any stand-in-for-the-genie in this metaphor, we can’t put it back in. Two options: (1) pure, unrelenting Darwinism, and (2) actually doing some work. Option 1: The environment as the teacher There is something fun about letting the slop detectives tear people to shreds. Authentication silently dropped? Headers not passed? Flags that do nothing? You’re publicly torn apart, and millions watch like they are enjoying an evening out at Tyburn. The consequences are immediate and public. We can think about this as reinforcement learning in its purest form. Not the version where you train a model in a sandbox. The real version, where the environment provides rewards and punishments, and products learn or die. Ship code that works, survive. Ship slop, get selected out. The environment doesn't care about your intentions or your process or how many fuzz harnesses you claim to have. Is this a good option? Yes, but mostly no. Yes, because it is bringing the problem to the forefront. Now, you generate an entire feature and ship it while concentrating on Factorio. Generation got fast. Verification didn't. Thus, verification gets skipped, so you can debug the bottleneck that actually matters: your iron smelting array. If you didn't verify it properly, you find out by Thursday. The loop has compressed from months to days. The Cortex 2026 Benchmark Report found that change failure rates increased 30% as teams ship more AI-generated code. More outages, more rollbacks. The environment is grading harshly, and most teams will learn quickly because this teacher is impossible to ignore. Pure Darwinism will teach these lessons. Expensively. But mostly no. For it to come to the forefront, there has to be a problem. AI slop is starting to drag down OSS projects. Both tldraw and Ghostty have limited issue creation due to the number of poor, AI-generated contributions they have received. Slop doesn’t just describe the quality of code; it also represents the quantity. There is now too much bad code, and it is screwing everything up. But this isn’t really a slop problem. In many ways, it isn’t even an AI problem. It is a human problem that needs to be solved with option two. Option 2: Actually doing some work The curl replacement wasn't bad because AI wrote it. It was bad because someone shipped unverified code into a domain that required decades of maturity and thought that was fine. The AI is incidental. The failure is human judgment. As Simon Willison puts it , "A computer can never be held accountable. That's your job as the human in the loop." Claude isn't going to get fired for the curl replacement. The AI has no reputation to protect, no career at stake, no skin in the game. Someone decided to ship that code. That person made a verification decision, or failed to make one. This is freeing once you accept it. You don't have to solve "how do we stop people from generating slop." That's not a solvable problem. The economics are too compelling. Code generation is cheap and fast, and people will use cheap and fast tools. The people building these tools understand this. Claude Code writes 80% of Claude Code. Claude Code writes 100% of Claude Cowork. And still: " Every line of code should be reviewed by an engineer. " Anthropic doesn't ship unverified AI output, even when the AI is building itself. The question is: how do you build systems that catch slop before it reaches users? Verification. Testing. Proof that code does what it claims to do. Grokking that the test is the truth . This isn't a new idea. It's the oldest idea in software engineering, finally getting the attention it deserves because the consequences of ignoring it are now immediate and visible. But it requires a shift. Verification can't be downstream. It can't be "QA will catch it" or "we'll add tests later." When code generation is instant, verification has to be instant too, and that’s as much an organizational shift as a technical one. It means treating specification as production work, and accepting that some features won’t ship because correctness was never defined. “We don’t know what right looks like yet” has to be an acceptable answer. The test comes first. The behavior contract comes first. Code is generated to satisfy the contract, not the other way around. This is where human judgment actually matters now. Not in writing the implementation. In defining what must be true. In specifying behavior precisely enough that correctness is verifiable. The differentiator isn't "can you write the code?" It's "Can you define what the code must do, clearly and completely?" What does this look like? Behavior tests that define outcomes, not implementation details Contracts at system boundaries, not just unit coverage Explicit ownership of what AI generates vs. what humans verify Failure modes that are enumerable, not emergent Observability designed in from the start, not bolted on after an incident Not every system can do all of this at once. Legacy code rarely has clear contract boundaries or well-defined enumerable failure modes. In practice, verification starts at the edges and moves inward. Verification is the first discipline, not the only one. Testing won’t save you if the architecture is chaos or the organization rewards speed over correctness. But you can’t fix incentives or culture while continuing to ship unverified code. AI just makes the cost of that failure arrive faster. The slop is out of the bottle, and we can’t put it back in. So let's work on decontamination.
